reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / WHO envenoming guidance
clinicalPearls: Broadly divide marine injuries into nematocyst stings (jellyfish and relatives) and venomous puncture wounds (fish spines, stingrays, urchins, cone snails)
For heat-stable venoms of many venomous fish, sea urchins and stingrays, hot-water immersion at a tolerable temperature relieves pain

For jellyfish stings, decontamination depends on species: vinegar is used for tropical box jellyfish/cubozoans, whereas indiscriminate use in other species may be unhelpful, and fresh water and rubbing should be avoided
Puncture wounds commonly retain spine or barb fragments, so imaging and wound exploration and irrigation are important
Marine wounds are prone to infection by marine organisms such as Vibrio species, so wound care, tetanus prophylaxis and vigilance for infection are essential

A small number of syndromes are rapidly life-threatening (Chironex cardiotoxicity, Irukandji cardiac failure, tetrodotoxin paralysis from blue-ringed octopus, sea snake neuro/myotoxicity), so resuscitation and monitoring come first
Specific antivenoms exist for a few marine species (box jellyfish, stonefish, sea snake); most stings are managed supportively
reference.pathophysiology: Marine venoms are delivered by two main mechanisms. Cnidarians (jellyfish, anemones, corals) fire nematocysts that inject venom on contact, with effects ranging from local pain and dermatitis to systemic cardiotoxicity or catecholamine-driven syndromes. Venomous fish, stingrays, sea urchins and cone snails introduce venom through spines, barbs or a radular tooth, causing intense local pain, tissue injury and, in some species, systemic neurotoxic or cardiovascular effects. Many fish and echinoderm venoms are heat-labile proteins, explaining the benefit of hot-water immersion, whereas cnidarian nematocyst discharge is influenced by osmotic and chemical changes, which underpins species-specific decontamination.
additionalDifferentials: Non-venomous marine laceration or abrasion with infection
Allergic or anaphylactic reaction to marine antigen
Decompression illness or immersion-related collapse in a diver
Seafood-borne toxin illness (ciguatera, scombroid, shellfish toxins)
Skin infection such as Vibrio, Mycobacterium marinum or Erysipelothrix
additionalInvestigations: Wound imaging (ultrasound or radiography) for retained spines or barbs
Neurovascular assessment of the affected part
Electrocardiography and monitoring where systemic toxicity is possible
Inflammatory markers and wound cultures if infection is suspected
Creatine kinase, renal function and haemolysis markers in significant systemic envenomation
Identification of the responsible species where possible to guide specific therapy
redFlags: Cardiovascular collapse or arrhythmia after a jellyfish sting
Delayed severe systemic syndrome after a trivial sting (Irukandji)
Spreading soft-tissue infection or systemic sepsis
Compartment syndrome or extensive necrosis around a puncture wound
reference.prognosis: Most marine envenomations cause self-limiting local pain and heal well with first aid and wound care. A minority of species cause life-threatening systemic toxicity, where outcome depends on prompt resuscitation, appropriate decontamination and, where available, species-specific antivenom.
pitfalls: Applying a single decontamination method to all jellyfish stings rather than species-appropriate treatment
Rinsing cnidarian stings with fresh water or rubbing them, provoking further nematocyst discharge
Missing retained spine fragments and marine wound infection during follow-up
Focusing on local wound care while overlooking rapidly evolving systemic toxicity
